{{short description|Function whose all derivatives vanish at a point}}
[[File:FBN exp(-1x2).jpeg|thumb|The graph of <math>f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>f(0)=0</math> and that for all <math>x\in\mathbb{R}</math>, <math>x\neq0</math> implies <math>f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}</math>]]
In [[real analysis]], a [[real function]] is defined to be '''flat''' at a point in its domain if all its [[higher-order derivative|derivatives]] or [[partial derivative|partial derivatives]] exist at that point and equal <math>0</math>.

A real function is [[locally constant function|''locally constant'']] (that is, constant in at least one [[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]]) of a point in the interior of its domain if and only if the function is flat and [[analytic function|analytic]] at that point.

An example of a function that is flat only at an [[isolated point]] is <math>f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>f(0)=0</math> and that for all <math>x\in\mathbb{R}</math>, <math>x\neq0</math> implies <math>f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}</math>; the function <math>f</math> is flat only at <math>0</math>.

Since <math>f</math> is not analytic at <math>0</math>, the extension of <math>f</math> to <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is not [[holomorphic function|holomorphic]] at <math>0</math>, since for complex functions, [[Holomorphic function|holomorphicity]] at a point implies [[Analytic function|analyticity]] at that point.

==Examples of construction of non-trivial flat functions==

By a non-trivial flat function, what is meant is a function that, at least at one point in the interior of its domain, is flat but not locally constant.

===Construction of univariate flat functions===

Let <math>a</math> be a positive real number and let <math>g:S\to\mathbb{R}</math> (where <math>S\subseteq\mathbb{R}</math> is a [[neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of a point <math>x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}</math>) be such that <math>g(x_{0})=0</math> and that for all <math>x\in S</math>, <math>x\neq x_{0}</math> implies <math>g(x)=\operatorname{exp}(-|x-x_{0}|^{-a}).</math>

Then <math>g</math> is flat at <math>x_{0}</math>.

===Construction of multivariate flat functions===

Let <math>G:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> be flat at <math>0</math>, and let <math>H:P\to\mathbb{R}</math> (where <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>, <math>\mathbf{x}_{0}</math> is an <math>n</math>-dimensional real [[coordinate vector]], and <math>P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> is a neighbourhood of <math>\mathbf{x}_{0}</math>) be such that for all <math>\mathbf{x}\in P</math>,<math>H(\mathbf{x})=G(||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{0}||)</math>, where for all <math>\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, <math>||\mathbf{p}||</math> denotes the [[l2 norm|Euclidean norm]] of <math>\mathbf{p}</math>.

Then <math>H</math> is flat at <math>\mathbf{x}_{0}</math>.

==A necessary condition for flatness and local non-constancy==

Let <math>S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> for some <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math> and let <math>F:S\to\mathbb{R}</math> be flat at a point <math>x_{0}</math> in the interior of <math>S</math>. Also let it be the case that for every neighbourhood <math>N</math> of <math>x_{0}</math>, there exists an <math>x\in N</math> such that <math>F(x)\neq F(x_{0})</math>, that is, that <math>F</math> is not locally constant at <math>x_{0}</math>. Then <math>F</math> is non-analytic at <math>x_{0}</math>.

===Proof===
Assume the contrary, that is, that <math>F</math> is analytic at <math>x_{0}</math>. Since <math>F</math> is flat at <math>x_{0}</math>, the [[Taylor series]] of <math>F</math> at <math>x_{0}</math> is constant and equal to <math>F(x_{0})</math>. Since it is assumed that <math>F</math> is analytic at <math>x_{0}</math>, then there exists a neighbourhood <math>N</math> of <math>x_{0}</math> such that for all <math>x\in N</math>, <math>F(x)=F(x_{0})</math>. This contradicts that for every neighbourhood <math>N</math> of <math>x_{0}</math>, there exists an <math>x\in N</math> such that <math>F(x)\neq F(x_{0})</math>. Hence, by contradiction, <math>F</math> is non-analytic at <math>x_{0}</math>.

==A sufficient condition for flatness==

Let <math>S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> for some <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math> and let <math>F:S\to\mathbb{R}</math> be infinitely differentiable at a point <math>x_{0}</math> in the interior of <math>S</math>. Also let it be the case that for every neighbourhood <math>N</math> of <math>x_{0}</math>, there exists an <math>x\in N</math> such that <math>F</math> is flat at <math>x</math>. Then <math>F</math> is flat at <math>x_{0}</math>.

===Proof===
Assume the contrary, that is, that <math>F</math> is not flat at <math>x_{0}</math>. Then there exists a <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math> such that a <math>k</math>-th partial derivative of <math>F</math> (call it <math>F_{k}</math>) is non-zero at <math>x_{0}</math>, that is, <math>F_{k}(x_{0})=r</math> for some <math>r\in\mathbb{R}</math> such that <math>r\neq0</math>. Since <math>F</math> is infinitely differentiable at <math>x_{0}</math>, then <math>F_{k}</math> is continuous at <math>x_{0}</math>. Since <math>r\neq0</math>, then <math>|r|/2>0</math>. Then there exists a neighbourhood <math>N</math> of <math>x_{0}</math> such that for all <math>x\in N</math>, <math>|F_{k}(x)-F_{k}(x_{0})|<|r|/2</math>, which means <math>|F_{k}(x)-r|<|r|/2</math>, or, in other words,  <math>F_{k}(x)</math> lies in the open interval <math>(\operatorname{min}\{r/2,3r/2\},\operatorname{max}\{r/2,3r/2\})</math>. Since <math>r\neq0</math>, <math>0\notin(\operatorname{min}\{r/2,3r/2\},\operatorname{max}\{r/2,3r/2\})</math>, so <math>F_{k}(x)\neq0</math>, which means that there exists a <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math> such that a <math>k</math>-th partial derivative of <math>F</math> is non-zero at <math>x</math>. This contradicts that <math>F</math> is flat at at least one point in every neighbourhood of <math>x_{0}</math>. Hence, by contradiction, <math>F</math> is flat at <math>x_{0}</math>.

The above results can be used to show that a [[bump function]] is flat and non-analytic at each boundary point of the closure of its [[support (mathematics)|support]].

==Flatness of smooth interpolations==

{{see also|Smoothness#Geometric continuity}}

Let <math>s_{1}\in\mathbb{R}</math> and <math>s_{2}\in\mathbb{R}</math> be such that <math>s_{1}<s_{2}</math>.

Let <math>I_{1}\subset\mathbb{R}</math> be an [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] with non-empty interior, with [[infimum and supremum|supremum]] <math>s_{1}</math>, and containing <math>s_{1}</math>; and let <math>I_{2}\subset\mathbb{R}</math> be an interval with non-empty interior, with [[infimum and supremum|infimum]] <math>s_{2}</math>, and containing <math>s_{2}</math>.

In the following, continuity, one-sided continuity, one-sided limits, differentiability and smoothness of a real coordinate vector-valued function are respectively given by continuity, one-sided continuity, one-sided limits, differentiability and smoothness of the function in each coordinate.

Let <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>. Let <math>\mathbf{r}_{1}:I_{1}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be continuously differentiable at every point in the interior of <math>I_{1}</math>, left-continuous at <math>s_{1}</math> and have the left-hand limit of its derivatives of all orders be finite at <math>s_{1}</math>; also let <math>||\mathbf{r}_{1}'(s)||=1</math> for all <math>s\in \operatorname{int}(I_{1})</math>. Let <math>\mathbf{r}_{2}:I_{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be continuously differentiable at every point in the interior of <math>I_{2}</math>, right-continuous at <math>s_{2}</math> and have the right-hand limit of its derivatives of all orders be finite at <math>s_{2}</math>; also let <math>||\mathbf{r}_{2}'(s)||=1</math> for all <math>s\in \operatorname{int}(I_{2})</math>.

Let curves <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math> be the images of the domains of <math>\mathbf{r}_{1}</math> and <math>\mathbf{r}_{2}</math>, respectively. Both <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math> inhabit <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>.

A smooth interpolation between <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math>, between the points <math>\mathbf{r}_{1}(s_{1})</math> and <math>\mathbf{r}_{2}(s_{2})</math>, is the image of the domain of a function <math>\mathbf{r}_{0}:(s_{1},s_{2})\to\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> such that the left-hand limit of <math>\mathbf{r}_{0}</math> at <math>s_{1}</math> is <math>\mathbf{r}_{1}(s_{1})</math>, the right-hand limit of <math>\mathbf{r}_{0}</math> at <math>s_{2}</math> is <math>\mathbf{r}_{2}(s_{2})</math>, and for all <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math>, the left-hand limit of the <math>k</math>-th derivative of <math>\mathbf{r}_{0}</math> at <math>s_{1}</math> is equal to the right-hand limit of the <math>k</math>-th derivative of <math>\mathbf{r}_{1}</math> at <math>s_{1}</math>, and the right-hand limit of the <math>k</math>-th derivative of <math>\mathbf{r}_{0}</math> at <math>s_{2}</math> is equal to the left-hand limit of the <math>k</math>-th derivative of <math>\mathbf{r}_{2}</math> at <math>s_{2}</math>. A smooth interpolation between <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math> is defined to have <math>G^{\infty}</math> continuity ([[smoothness#geometric continuity|geometric continuity]] of all orders) with <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math>.

Let <math>\mathbf{r}:I_{1}\cup(s_{1},s_{2})\cup I_{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> be such that: for all <math>s\in I_{1}</math>, <math>\mathbf{r}(s)=\mathbf{r}_{1}(s)</math>; for all <math>s\in(s_{1},s_{2})</math>, <math>\mathbf{r}(s)=\mathbf{r}_{0}(s)</math>; and for all <math>s\in I_{2}</math>, <math>\mathbf{r}(s)=\mathbf{r}_{2}(s)</math>.

If <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math> are straight line segments, <math>\mathbf{r}</math> is necessarily flat at <math>s_{1}</math> and <math>s_{2}</math>. If <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math> are non-collinear straight line segments, there necessarily exists a point in <math>[s_{1},s_{2}]</math> at which <math>\mathbf{r}</math> is non-analytic. If the end segments of the smooth interpolation are not straight-segment extensions of line segments <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_{2}</math>, <math>\mathbf{r}</math> is necessarily non-analytic at <math>s_{1}</math> and <math>s_{2}</math>.
